title: About SEVS | SEVS
description: Specialist Endovascular Services is a group of doctors trained in minimally invasive treatment of vascular disease.
heading: About SEVS
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

Specialist Endovascular Services is a group of doctors trained in minimally invasive treatment of vascular disease.

Who we are

SEVS is a group of specially trained doctors who use endovascular techniques to treat vascular diseases including brain aneurysms, stroke and arteriovenous malformations.

Endovascular treatment is an alternative to open surgery for many vascular conditions and may offer smaller incisions, faster recovery and improved outcomes. The appropriate treatment depends on each patient’s anatomy, condition and clinical circumstances.

We provide emergency services at Westmead Hospital and Royal North Shore Hospital, and elective care through several major Sydney hospitals.

Patient-centred decision making

We work closely with neurosurgical, neurological, vascular and other specialist colleagues and recommend endovascular or open treatment according to best medical practice.

title: Aneurysm Management | SEVS
description: Assessment and treatment options for intracranial aneurysms.
heading: Aneurysm Management
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

Assessment and treatment options for intracranial aneurysms.

A brain aneurysm is a focal weakness or outpouching of an artery. Management depends on rupture status, aneurysm size and shape, location, patient age and individual risk factors.

Treatment options

  • Observation with interval imaging
  • Endovascular coiling
  • Flow-diverting stents
  • Intrasaccular devices
  • Microsurgical clipping

Every aneurysm requires individual assessment. A consultation should explain the natural history, treatment options and material risks.

Specialist Endovascular Services

Minimally invasive diagnosis and treatment of vascular conditions affecting the brain, head, neck and spine.

What is interventional neuroradiology?

Interventional neuroradiology uses image guidance, catheters and specialised devices to diagnose and treat vascular conditions from within the blood vessels.

Diagnostic procedures

Cerebral angiography and specialised vascular imaging.

Treatments

Coiling, flow diversion, embolisation, angioplasty, stenting and mechanical thrombectomy.

title: Medical Glossary | SEVS
description: Plain-language definitions of common endovascular terms.
heading: Medical Glossary
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

Plain-language definitions of common endovascular terms.

Angiogram
An X-ray study of blood vessels using contrast.
Catheter
A thin flexible tube guided through blood vessels.
Coil
A small implant used to reduce blood flow into an aneurysm or vessel.
Embolisation
Blocking a blood vessel or abnormal vascular connection from within.
Flow diverter
A specialised stent used to redirect blood flow away from an aneurysm.
Thrombectomy
Mechanical removal of a blood clot, commonly in acute ischaemic stroke.

title: Frequently Asked Questions | SEVS
description: Answers to common questions about appointments and procedures.
heading: Frequently Asked Questions
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

Answers to common questions about appointments and procedures.

How do I schedule an appointment?

Contact our rooms after your referral has been sent.

How long does a diagnostic cerebral angiogram take?

The procedure commonly takes about one hour, followed by several hours of recovery. Timing varies.

Do I need to stop medications?

Do not stop medicines unless instructed. Tell the team about diabetes medicines, anticoagulants and antiplatelet medicines.

Will I need to fast?

Follow the specific fasting instructions provided for your procedure.

Can I drive home?

You will commonly need an adult to accompany you home and stay overnight after sedation or angiography.

title: Potential Risks | SEVS
description: Understanding benefits, alternatives and risks is an essential part of consent.
heading: Potential Risks
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

Understanding benefits, alternatives and risks is an essential part of consent.

All medical procedures carry risk. The specific risks depend on the condition, procedure, access route, devices used and the patient’s overall health.

  • Bleeding or bruising at the access site
  • Allergic reaction or kidney injury from contrast
  • Blood vessel injury or blockage
  • Stroke, neurological injury or other organ injury
  • Need for further treatment or surgery

This page is general information only. Your specialist will discuss procedure-specific risks and alternatives before treatment.

title: Varicocele Embolisation | SEVS
description: A minimally invasive treatment for symptomatic varicoceles.
heading: Varicocele Embolisation
html:
Specialist Endovascular Services

A minimally invasive treatment for symptomatic varicoceles.

Varicocele embolisation blocks abnormal veins around the testicle using a catheter inserted through a small puncture. It may be considered for pain, infertility or recurrence after surgery.

What to expect

The procedure is generally performed with local anaesthetic and sedation. Most patients return home the same day, depending on clinical circumstances.

Assessment and embolisation of arteriovenous and other vascular malformations.

Vascular malformations are abnormal connections or formations of arteries, veins, capillaries or lymphatic vessels. They can occur in the brain, spine, head and neck or elsewhere in the body.

Management

Treatment may involve observation, embolisation, surgery, radiosurgery or a combination of techniques, guided by a multidisciplinary team.

title: Conditions | SEVS
description: Neurovascular and vascular conditions assessed and treated by Specialist Endovascular Services.
heading: Conditions
html:
Conditions

Information about neurovascular and vascular conditions assessed by the SEVS team.

Our specialists assess vascular disorders of the brain, head and neck, spine and selected vascular conditions elsewhere in the body. Diagnosis commonly combines clinical assessment with CT, MRI, ultrasound and, where required, catheter angiography.

Brain aneurysms

Assessment of ruptured and unruptured intracranial aneurysms, including surveillance and endovascular treatment options.

Learn about brain aneurysms →

Carotid artery stenosis

Narrowing of the carotid arteries caused most commonly by atherosclerosis, with assessment focused on stroke risk, symptoms and stenosis severity.

Learn about carotid stenosis →

Arteriovenous malformations

Abnormal high-flow connections between arteries and veins affecting the brain, spine or other tissues.

Learn about AVMs →

Dural arteriovenous fistula

Abnormal connections between arteries and veins within the dura that may present with pulsatile tinnitus or neurological symptoms.

Learn about dural AV fistula →

Pulsatile tinnitus

A pulse-synchronous sound that can have an underlying vascular cause and may require targeted vascular imaging.

Learn about pulsatile tinnitus →

Vascular malformations

Venous, lymphatic and arteriovenous malformations can occur throughout the body and may require MRI, ultrasound or angiographic assessment.

Learn about vascular malformations →

Information, not individual medical advice

These pages provide general information. Investigation and treatment decisions depend on symptoms, imaging, anatomy, age and individual clinical circumstances.

title: Carotid Artery Stenosis | Investigation & Treatment | SEVS
description: Patient information about carotid artery stenosis, stroke risk, investigations including ultrasound, CTA and MRA, and contemporary treatment options.
heading: Carotid Artery Stenosis
html:
Conditions · Cerebrovascular disease

Carotid stenosis is narrowing of the major arteries in the neck that supply blood to the brain.

What is carotid stenosis?

Carotid artery stenosis is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation. Plaque can reduce the diameter of the artery and can also release clot or debris into the cerebral circulation, causing a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or ischaemic stroke.

Symptoms

Many carotid stenoses are discovered before they cause symptoms. A stenosis is considered symptomatic when it is associated with a recent, clinically relevant retinal or cerebral ischaemic event in the territory supplied by that artery. Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, speech disturbance, facial weakness or sudden loss of vision in one eye requires urgent medical assessment.

How is it investigated?

Carotid duplex ultrasound

A non-invasive first-line test that evaluates plaque and blood-flow velocities. The degree of stenosis is estimated from velocity criteria and the appearance of the vessel.

CT angiography (CTA)

Provides high-resolution assessment from the aortic arch through the neck and intracranial circulation. It is useful for confirming stenosis, evaluating calcification, tandem disease and procedural anatomy.

MR angiography (MRA)

Provides vascular assessment without ionising radiation and may be useful when CTA is unsuitable. The optimal MR technique depends on the clinical question and patient factors.

Catheter angiography

Digital subtraction angiography provides detailed vascular anatomy and is generally reserved for selected cases, uncertainty on non-invasive imaging, or when an endovascular procedure is being planned.

Additional brain imaging

CT or MRI of the brain can identify previous infarction and help determine whether symptoms are consistent with carotid disease. In selected patients, perfusion or cerebrovascular-reserve assessment may be useful when haemodynamic compromise is a concern; these tests answer a different question from simply measuring the percentage stenosis.

How is severity assessed?

Management should not be based on a single ultrasound number in isolation. The measured degree of narrowing, plaque morphology, confirmatory vascular imaging, symptoms, timing of symptoms, intracranial circulation and the patient’s overall health all contribute to risk assessment. When intervention is contemplated, confirmation with high-quality CTA or MRA is commonly appropriate, particularly where duplex findings are uncertain or discordant.

Treatment

All patients require attention to vascular risk factors. This may include antiplatelet therapy when appropriate, lipid lowering, blood-pressure control, diabetes management and smoking cessation. Revascularisation is considered for selected patients where the expected stroke-prevention benefit outweighs procedural risk.

Carotid endarterectomy

Open surgery removes plaque from the carotid artery. It remains an established treatment, particularly for many patients with recently symptomatic severe stenosis.

Carotid artery stenting

An endovascular approach in which a stent is placed across the stenosis. Patient selection considers age, anatomy, surgical risk, prior neck treatment and operator/institutional experience. Both transfemoral and transcarotid approaches may be considered in contemporary practice.

Current guideline principles

Contemporary international guidelines consistently emphasise optimal medical therapy for all patients and timely revascularisation for appropriately selected patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis. For asymptomatic disease, intervention is more selective because modern medical therapy has reduced baseline stroke risk; stenosis severity alone is not sufficient to determine treatment.

Urgent symptoms

New stroke or TIA symptoms are an emergency. Call 000 or attend an emergency department rather than waiting for an outpatient appointment.

Clinical content should be reviewed periodically as carotid evidence and guidelines evolve. Last website content review: August 2026.

title: Brain Aneurysms | SEVS
description: Information about brain aneurysms, investigation, rupture risk, surveillance and treatment options.
heading: Brain Aneurysms
html:
Conditions · Neurovascular

Information about brain aneurysms, investigation, rupture risk, surveillance and treatment options.

Ruptured and unruptured aneurysms

A ruptured aneurysm causes subarachnoid haemorrhage and requires emergency specialist treatment. Unruptured aneurysms are often discovered incidentally and require an individual assessment of future rupture risk against the risks of treatment.

Investigation

CTA and MRA can identify and follow many aneurysms. Catheter angiography remains important when very detailed anatomy is required or an endovascular procedure is planned.

Management

Options can include imaging surveillance, endovascular coiling, flow diversion or other endovascular devices, and microsurgical clipping.

Brain aneurysm treatment information

title: Brain Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM) | SEVS
description: Information about cerebral arteriovenous malformations, imaging and treatment options.
heading: Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)
html:
Conditions · Neurovascular

Information about cerebral arteriovenous malformations, imaging and treatment options.

Presentation and diagnosis

Brain AVMs may be discovered after haemorrhage, seizures, headache or incidentally. MRI and CTA help define the lesion; catheter angiography provides detailed information about arterial supply, the nidus and venous drainage.

Management

Options can include observation, endovascular embolisation, microsurgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, or a combination of treatments.

AVM treatment information

title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula | SEVS
description: Information about dural arteriovenous fistulas, symptoms, imaging and endovascular treatment.
heading: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula
html:
Conditions · Neurovascular

Information about dural arteriovenous fistulas, symptoms, imaging and endovascular treatment.

Symptoms

Presentation varies with location and venous drainage. Pulsatile tinnitus is common in some fistulas; others can cause neurological symptoms, visual problems or intracranial haemorrhage.

Investigation

CTA or MRI/MRA may suggest a fistula. Catheter cerebral angiography is often required to fully define arterial feeders and venous drainage because these features determine risk and treatment strategy.

Treatment

Many clinically significant dAVFs can be treated endovascularly by embolising the abnormal connection.

Dural AV fistula treatment

title: Pulsatile Tinnitus | SEVS
description: Information about pulse-synchronous tinnitus and investigation for vascular causes.
heading: Pulsatile Tinnitus
html:
Conditions · Neurovascular

Information about pulse-synchronous tinnitus and investigation for vascular causes.

Why vascular assessment matters

Unlike common non-pulsatile tinnitus, pulse-synchronous tinnitus can sometimes arise from an arterial or venous abnormality. Causes range from benign venous variants to conditions such as dural arteriovenous fistula or venous sinus stenosis.

Investigation

Imaging may include MRI/MRA/MRV, CTA/CTV or targeted temporal-bone imaging. Catheter angiography is reserved for selected patients when a vascular lesion remains suspected or detailed anatomy is required.

Treatment

Treatment is directed at the underlying cause.
